newsitem.title: FIJI: Fiji's new, non-racial constitution becomes law.
newsitem.headline: Fiji's new, non-racial constitution becomes law.

text.p: Fiji's new, non-racial constitution became law on Friday, replacing race-based laws which guaranteed native Fijians control of the parliament and prevented non-indigenous Fijians from holding high office.

Fiji President Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara signed into law the South Pacific nation's new constitution, replacing a seven-year-old racially-biased charter which saw Fiji expelled from the Commonwealth in 1990.
However, the new constitution will not come into effect until July 27, 1998.
"I feel good, I feel great. We have achieved our objective...," Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka told reporters.
Rabuka staged a military coup in 1987, overthrowing the government then dominated by ethnic Indians, and subsequently introduced the racially-biased constitution.
The Fijian parliament approved the new constitution earlier this month, but Rabuka has said he will not seek to form a multi-racial government until after the next election in 1999.

"It's indeed a remarkable day and hopefully having achieved this we can move in the same direction that we have set ourselves, which is unity of all the people...," said Jai Ram Reddy, head of the Indian-dominated opposition.
"The sooner there is an election under the constitution the better," Reddy said.

A new 71-seat parliament will see 23 guaranteed Fijian seats, 19 Indian seats, three for mixed races, one for Rotuma Islanders and 25 seats open to all races. It also permits a non-indigenous Fijian to become prime minister.

Indians, who were brought to Fiji at the turn of the century to work on sugar plantations, now make up 45 percent of the country's 750,000-strong population and are influential in the business community.
